name: The Night Watchman
role: The office's security: how it stands, and what is unusually different
greet.4: Hear, you people, and let me tell you …
fit.yes: Every server can use a watch at night. His first check records what is there — from then on it is known.
fire_note: Nothing keeps running: he stops checking, his watch book stays. Hire him again and he learns afresh what is there.
bubble.first: My first round is still to come. Then I note what is normal.

bubble.open.one: One thing waits for your answer.

bubble.syslog_full: /var/log is full — the syslog no longer grows, so I see no logins or restarts in it. Last round {when}.
bubble.vuln_off: Shall I also check once a day whether an actively exploited vulnerability hits something here? I'd fetch public lists for it — nothing of your server goes along.
vuln.switch_on_title: Once a day public lists (cisa.gov, raw.githubusercontent.com, releases.unraid.net, endoflife.date; for what stays unclear nvd.nist.gov) — nothing of your server goes along, to the NVD only the vulnerability's number
vuln.on: Known vulnerabilities on — the lists come with his next look.
vuln.kev_line: He compares with the list of the US agency CISA: vulnerabilities known to be exploited. It has been kept since November 2021.

vuln.counted.other: {n} of the list's {total} vulnerabilities concern programs he checks here: {list}.

vuln.counted_none: None of the list's {total} vulnerabilities concerns a program he checks here.

vuln.pending.one: For one of them he is still fetching the description (at most 60 a day); until then it stands in no list.
vuln.pending.other: For {n} of them he is still fetching the description (at most 60 a day); until then they stand in no list.

vuln.router_seen: {product} {version}: as its log has said since {date}.
vuln.router_unknown: {product}: version unknown — he only sees it once the router writes it into its log.
vuln.not_sub: These vulnerabilities hit programs that run here. Your version is already patched, or it was never affected.
vuln.unsure_sub: Whether these vulnerabilities concern your version, he can't say for sure — each line says why. So he doesn't tell them and doesn't count them.
vuln.old_sub: Fixed in versions older than anything that runs from Unraid {floor} on. The office doesn't install on anything older.
vuln.unsure_nvd_asked: Neither the record nor the NVD names versions he can compare with yours.
vuln.unsure_nvd_wait: The record's versions can't be compared with yours; he is still checking with the NVD (at most 40 vulnerabilities a day).
vuln.unsure_why_rough: The list names the version only roughly (up to {bound}) — whether your patch level belongs to it, he can't say.
vuln.unsure_why_eol: Your release line {line} got no more updates when the vulnerability became known. The vendor doesn't check such lines.
vuln.unsure_why_lower: Here he sees only the version it started from ({have}) — it may have updated itself since. Whether the vulnerability concerns the one running now, he can't say.
vuln.limits: He can't look everywhere, so he never sees everything. He compares only with vulnerabilities publicly listed as actively exploited (CISA's list), not with every published one — and only for the programs he knows by name and whose version he can read. What nobody has published yet, he can't know. «Nothing found» therefore means: nothing found in what he could check — never «safe».
vuln.look_sub: What he read at his last look, and what he doesn't see.
vuln.look_ct_none: Docker didn't answer at his last look: no container checked.

vuln.look_unread_none.one: One container he couldn't check: its image names no version he can read — {names}.
vuln.look_unread_none.other: {n} containers he couldn't check: their images name no version he can read — {names}.

vuln.look_unread_unasked.one: One container whose image he couldn't read this time — {names}.
vuln.look_unread_unasked.other: {n} containers whose images he couldn't read this time — {names}.

vuln.look_unread_more.one: And one more container he couldn't check.
vuln.look_unread_more.other: And {n} more containers he couldn't check.

vuln.look_inside: He doesn't look inside a container.
vuln.look_routers_none: No router whose log comes here is one he knows (MikroTik RouterOS, UniFi Network).
vuln.look_not_vm: Virtual machines: he never looks inside one.

vuln.look_not_vm_n.one: One virtual machine: he never looks inside it.
vuln.look_not_vm_n.other: {n} virtual machines: he never looks inside one.

vuln.look_not_vm_none: No VMs. Inside one he would never look.
vuln.look_not_net: Other devices on your network — computers, phones, printers, cameras. A router only by the version its own log says.
vuln.look_not_inside: In a container, only what its image declares itself (for Synology DSM in virtual-dsm: the build its storage folder names) — whatever else it brings along he doesn't see.
vuln.look_not_other: Programs that aren't on his list of names he doesn't compare at all, even when they run here.
vuln.look_plugins: Plugins he doesn't compare themselves. A package a plugin installs counts when its name is on his list (OpenSSH, Samba, nginx …).
vuln.nvd_notice: This product uses the NVD API but is not endorsed or certified by the NVD.

vuln.down.one: {source} hasn't answered for a day — he tries again on {when}.
vuln.down.other: {source} hasn't answered for {n} days — he tries again on {when}.

vuln.down_nvd.one: Until then one vulnerability stays under «Can't be checked for sure».
vuln.down_nvd.other: Until then {n} vulnerabilities stay under «Can't be checked for sure».

vuln.down_cve: New vulnerabilities of the list stay without a description until then.
vuln.down_kev: The list of vulnerabilities is from {date}.
vuln.down_unraid: What he knows of Unraid's releases is from {date}.
vuln.down_eol: What he knows of how long software gets updates is from {date}.
vuln.explain_lists: Switched on, he fetches public lists once a day: the vulnerabilities known to be exploited (CISA, cisa.gov), the record of each of them (CVE, raw.githubusercontent.com), Unraid's releases with their support (releases.unraid.net) and how long software versions get updates (endoflife.date). What a record doesn't settle he asks the NVD (services.nvd.nist.gov), with the vulnerability's number alone, at most 40 vulnerabilities a day.
vuln.explain_here: He compares them with what runs here: the Unraid version, the kernel, PHP, the installed packages (OpenSSH, OpenSSL, Samba, sudo, Bash, polkit, nginx …) and, in Docker images, the software versions they declare themselves (PHP, nginx, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Redis, Valkey, MongoDB, Node.js, Python, Go, Java, Apache HTTP Server, Apache Tomcat, Elasticsearch, Kibana, Jenkins, n8n, Roundcube, Zabbix frontend, phpMyAdmin, Nextcloud, Vaultwarden, Paperless-ngx, Immich, Plex Media Server, Jellyfin, Emby Server, Home Assistant, AdGuard Home, UniFi Network), and Synology DSM in virtual-dsm by the build its storage folder names. Nothing of your server goes along — only the request itself.
vuln.explain_says: «Affected» he says only when the versions compare cleanly. What can't be compared stands calmly under «Can't be checked for sure», without an entry and without a notification. Off again: in his setup, «Known vulnerabilities» → «Watch this area».
vuln.switch_title: On: the public lists once a day, compared with what runs here — nothing of your server goes along. Off: nothing is fetched any more.
vuln.off_done: Known vulnerabilities off — nothing is fetched any more.

Update: Unraid itself and its parts (kernel, PHP, Samba, OpenSSH …) under ⟦Tools⟧ → ⟦Update OS⟧, a container through its image. The entry names the fixed version where the record says one.

posture.unraid_eol.title: Unraid {version} gets no more security updates
posture.unraid_eol.why: Unraid's own list of releases says «{status}» for {version}: fixes come only with a newer release (the newest supported one: {newest}). Vulnerabilities found from now on stay open here. Update under ⟦Tools⟧ → ⟦Update OS⟧.

posture.software_eol.title.one: Software past its end in a container: {names}
posture.software_eol.title.other: {n} programs past their end in containers: {names}

posture.software_eol.why: These release lines get no more fixes (endoflife.date), not even for security — whatever is found from now on stays open in these containers. A newer image of the container usually brings a newer line: update the container, or pick an image tag of a supported release.
round_now_title: Check right away instead of waiting for the next check
round_failed: The check went wrong — the messenger's log says why.
round_stopped: The check took too long and was stopped — nothing new was read. He tries again next time.
notify_off: No more reports to Unraid's notifications. All of it stays in the watch book.
notify_missing: Unraid's notification script isn't there — he can't report anything.
round.title: The last check
round.sub: Every five minutes, also with the office closed. He reads only RAM, the flash and disks that are awake; no disk wakes up for him.
stat.open_tip: Show only these in the watch book — a second click shows all of it again
round.first: At his first check, everything there now becomes known. Nothing is told for it.
round.failed: The last check went wrong — the messenger's log says why. He tries again next time.
round.stopped: The last check took too long and was stopped — what it would have read is still to come. He tries again at the next check.
round.skipped: The syslog grew by more than {size} since the check before — he read the newest part only.
round.no_docker: Docker didn't answer at the last check — containers were left out.
round.syslog_full: /var/log is full ({free} free of {total}) — the syslog no longer grows: logins, failed logins and restarts go unseen until there is room again. Ms. Protocolli shows what fills it.
round.no_shares: Unraid's list of shares was missing at the last check — shares were left out.
posture.title: Advice
posture.sub: How it stands now and what he would set differently. Advice is not an alarm and doesn't go to Unraid's notifications; «I know, thanks» puts it aside until something changes.
posture.none: Nothing to say. It stands well.
posture.show_again_title: Count it again: in my bubble and at the team lead
posture.ack_title: Put it aside for every browser — it comes back when what it is about changes
posture.level_info_text: Can be right as it is — as long as you know.

posture.public.title.one: Open to everyone in the network: {names}
posture.public.title.other: {n} shares open to everyone in the network: {names}

posture.public.why: ⟦Security⟧ «⟦Public⟧»: anyone in your network may read, write and delete there — every device, every guest, every infected laptop. Set it to «⟦Secure⟧» (everyone reads, chosen users write) or «⟦Private⟧», and give your users access. A disk or a pool counts too; the flash has a tip of its own.
posture.telnet.title: Telnet is on
posture.telnet.why: Telnet sends everything unencrypted, the root password too. SSH does the same, encrypted. Switch Telnet off under ⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Management Access⟧.
posture.upnp.title: UPnP is on
posture.upnp.why: UPnP lets the server open ports on your router by itself — for Unraid Connect or WireGuard, without asking you. Every port it opens is a door from the internet, and nobody sees it. Open the ports you really need by hand on the router and switch UPnP off under ⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Management Access⟧.
posture.remote_access.title: The WebGUI is reachable from the internet
posture.remote_access.why: Unraid Connect's remote access is on ({type}, port {port}): whoever has the address reaches your login page. Good when you need it — then a long root password and two-factor login on your Unraid account. Switch it off when you don't use it.
posture.ftp.title: Unraid's FTP server is on
posture.ftp.why: FTP sends passwords and files unencrypted. If you don't need it, switch it off; for files over the network SMB or SFTP (comes with SSH) are the better choice.

posture.api_admin.title.one: An API key that can do everything: {names}
posture.api_admin.title.other: {n} API keys that can do everything: {names}

posture.api_admin.why: Whoever holds it can do over the network what root can in the web UI — stop the array, remove containers and VMs, install plugins; Unraid's API (/graphql) asks for nothing but the key, and the keys lie in clear on the flash. If nothing needs it any more, revoke it under ⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Management Access⟧ → ⟦API Keys⟧. An app that only reads gets a key with just the permissions it needs. A key that may make keys counts too: it can give itself everything.
posture.mitigations_off.title: CPU protection switched off (mitigations=off)
posture.mitigations_off.why: Your {cpu} boots without the protections against Spectre-like flaws; open now: {open}. That gives a few percent of speed (much more on older Intel, less on newer CPUs and AMD). Off is fine when only you and programs you trust run here. On is better as soon as VMs or containers run code you don't control, others use the server, or services are reachable from the internet. AMD is affected too — by its own flaws (e.g. SRSO, Retbleed, TSA). To switch on: remove «mitigations=off» under ⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Boot Parameters⟧, then reboot.

posture.vmscape.title.one: VMScape: a VM could read the host
posture.vmscape.title.other: VMScape: {n} VMs could read the host

posture.vmscape.why: This 2025 flaw lets a guest read memory of the host's VM process (QEMU) — exactly what the switched-off protection would cover. With VMs only you use it matters little; with VMs others use, or that run untrusted software, switch the protection back on.
posture.privileged.why: A privileged container may do nearly anything on the server — fine for tools that need it (hardware, VPN, the backup), worth a second look for everything else. On the Docker page: ⟦Edit⟧ → ⟦Privileged⟧ off, and see whether it still works. If a container turns privileged later, he notes it as an entry.

posture.privileged.quiet.one: Also privileged, but stopped and without ⟦Autostart⟧: {quiet}
posture.privileged.quiet.other: Also privileged, but stopped and without ⟦Autostart⟧: {quiet}

posture.as_last_seen: {docker} — this is how it looked at the last check that reached Docker.
posture.mitigations_on.title: CPU protection is on
posture.mitigations_on.why: Your {cpu} runs with the protections against Spectre-like flaws — the safe default. It costs a few percent of speed, more on older Intel CPUs. Switching it off only pays when nothing here runs code you don't trust and nothing is reachable from the internet.

check.quiet: The night watchman's watch book has nothing open
check.quiet_how: Whatever he finds different from normal shows up here until you note it on his page.

check.open.one: The night watchman has one open incident
check.open.other: The night watchman has {n} open incidents

check.open_how: They are on his list, each with what it is and what to do — note them there. «I know, thanks» here notes every one of them; a new one brings this line back.

check.posture.one: The night watchman has one security recommendation
check.posture.other: The night watchman has {n} security recommendations

check.posture_how: On his page under «How secure does it stand?» — each with why and where in Unraid. Advice, not something to do.

check.login_new_ip.one: Login from a new address: {user} from {ip} ({service})
check.login_new_ip.other: {n} logins from new addresses, the newest: {user} from {ip} ({service})

check.login_new_ip_how: If that was you (a new device, a VPN), «All right, remember this» on the night watchman's page adds the address to the known ones. If not: change root's password and check who can reach the server from outside (⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Management Access⟧, port forwardings on your router).

check.login_failures.other: Failed logins from {n} addresses, the newest: {ip} ({service})

check.login_failures_how: Someone tried to log in and failed again and again. A device of yours with an old password? Correct it there. An address from outside: the server can be reached from the internet — close the port forwarding or put a VPN in front. Unraid locks the WebGUI login of an address for 15 minutes after three failures.

check.container_new.other: {n} new containers with special rights, the newest: {name} ({rights})

check.container_new_how: A container with such rights reaches deep into the server. Installed on purpose: «All right, remember this» on the night watchman's page. If not: look at it under Docker and remove it.

check.container_privileged.other: {n} containers now run privileged, the newest: {name}

check.container_privileged_how: A privileged container can do nearly anything on the server. Switched on yourself (⟦Docker⟧ → the container → ⟦Edit⟧ → ⟦Privileged⟧): «All right, remember this». If not: switch it off again.

check.container_host.other: {n} containers now use the host directly, the newest: {name} ({rights})

check.container_host_how: With the host's network or processes a container sees the server itself. Intended: «All right, remember this». If not: set its network type back under ⟦Docker⟧ → the container → ⟦Edit⟧.

check.container_ports.other: {n} containers publish new ports, the newest: {name} ({rights})

check.container_ports_how: New ports make the app reachable in your network — and from outside through a port forwarding. Intended: «All right, remember this».

check.container_rights.other: {n} containers have new rights, the newest: {name} ({rights})

check.container_rights_how: Capabilities, devices or the Docker socket give a container more power over the server. Intended: «All right, remember this». If not: remove them under ⟦Docker⟧ → the container → ⟦Edit⟧.
check.plugin_new_how: A plugin runs as root on the server. Installed it yourself: «All right, remember this» on the night watchman's page. If not: remove it under ⟦Plugins⟧.

check.plugin_source.other: {n} plugins update from somewhere else now, the newest: {name} from {source}

check.plugin_source_how: The plugin takes its updates from another place now — usually the author moved. Check that it is still the same project, then «All right, remember this».
check.flash_go_how: /boot/config/go runs as root at every start of the server. Changed it yourself: «All right, remember this». If not: look at it in a terminal (the night watchman never reads its text).

check.flash_extra.one: A file in /boot/extra is new or changed: {file}
check.flash_extra.other: {n} files in /boot/extra are new or changed, the newest: {file}

check.flash_extra_how: Packages in /boot/extra are installed at every start of the server. Put there by you: «All right, remember this». If not: remove it.

check.flash_user.other: {n} new users on the flash, the newest: {user}

check.flash_user_how: Users are added under ⟦Users⟧. Added yourself: «All right, remember this». If not: remove the user.
check.flash_password_how: Changed it yourself (⟦Users⟧): «All right, remember this». If not: set a new password for this user right away.

check.flash_ssh_key.other: {n} new SSH keys, the newest for {user}: {key}

check.flash_ssh_key_how: A key lets its owner log in by SSH without a password. Yours: «All right, remember this». If not: remove it under ⟦Users⟧ → the user → ⟦SSH authorized keys⟧.

help.book_text: Every entry is something that was different from usual: when, what, from where. Open ones wait in their area for your answer and count on his tiles; the watch book holds what is done. Entries of the same kind on the same day share one row; «All …: all right» settles them together. Open ones stay until you answer; what you answered and incidents stay {days} days in the watch book (at most {keep} entries). What he settled himself or doesn't tell because it is always all right goes into his history at the bottom after a quiet week.
help.ack_text: He remembers what the entry names, as it is now. After that he only tells what changes again.
help.normal_text: At his first check after hiring he remembers what is there and tells nothing for it, also the login addresses in the syslog. That stands in each area under «Known», and what you answer with «All right, remember this» joins it. Hire him again later and he takes a fresh look.
help.round_text: He checks every five minutes in the background, also with the office closed. «Check now» doesn't wait for it.
help.logins_text: WebGUI and SSH logins: one from a new address, or {burst} or more failed ones from one address within {minutes} minutes. He keeps the names tried only when they are users of this server.
help.containers_text: A container gets more rights: privileged, the host's network or processes, new ports, capabilities, devices or the Docker socket. A new one only counts with such rights.
help.plugins_text: A new plugin, or one that takes its updates from another place now (the host; on GitHub and the like also the owner).
help.office_text: What the office set up itself is a plain line, never a report: a plugin the consultant installed, a container from the form he prepared, the throwaway containers of Mr. Restori's drill, and the lines the office writes into its own cron files, for itself and for each desk. A job a removed plugin left in atd's queue is a plain line too, as long as it is unchanged; it ends with the next reboot. Anything else is reported.
help.flash_text: /boot/config/go, /boot/extra, users, passwords and SSH keys. Of go he keeps only new lines, of passwords only a fingerprint, never the text.
help.shares_text: A share (also a disk, a pool or the flash) that guests now reach without a password, over SMB or NFS — as Unraid applies it.
help.notify_text: Important things go to Unraid's notifications right away; he bundles the same kind, at most once an hour. The switch under «Schedule» turns that off. What comes in that time is never told later either.
help.safe_text: He changes nothing on the server and wakes no disk: he reads only RAM, the flash and disks that are awake. What Fix Common Problems checks, he doesn't check again.

help.flow_text: Who pulls how much, every five minutes from the server's own counters: per client and service (SMB, NFS, SSH, WebGUI), per container, and per share what was written. On ZFS rewritten files count too, because that is how ransomware works. He learns over {keep} days what is usual at which hour. Unusual is {factor} × more than usual and at least {min} in the hour. During the first {learn} days he tells only clear cases: more than {new} between two checks, or {part} % of a share. «All right, remember this» raises what is usual. Expected are backups, the offsite upload, restores and media servers streaming. For SMB he also tells new users and machines. Sleeping pools are left alone.
help.flow_gone_text: What vanished from a share between two checks, deleted or moved — as untypical as mass writing. On ZFS he measures per share, on XFS and btrfs per disk. He also counts deleted files: unusual from {files_min} in the hour, while still learning from {files_new} in one check. During the first {learn} days he tells only when {new} or {part} % of a share vanish between two checks. Each entry says who was moving data over SMB, NFS or SSH at that moment. Not a loss: the work of the office, the mover, Jack Streamer and Ms. Dustdevil. Sleeping pools are never woken.
help.flow_not_text: Which files were read, and where data goes on the internet, he can't see. For that he would have to switch on logging that fills Unraid's small /var/log or is for experts only. He never does.
help.posture_text: At every check he looks at how the server stands: an open flash, shares open to everyone, Telnet, UPnP, the WebGUI from the internet, the FTP server, the CPU's protection against Spectre, and privileged containers. An advice is no alarm and sends no notification: it stands in its area, says why and has a link into Unraid. «I know, thanks» holds for every browser until something changes.

posture.flash.why: Even reading is too much here: the flash holds every user's password hash (/boot/config/shadow) and the SSH keys (/boot/config/ssh) — anyone in your network could copy them and try the passwords at leisure. On the flash's page (⟦Main⟧ → ⟦Flash⟧) set ⟦Export⟧ to «⟦No⟧» under ⟦SMB Security Settings⟧ — or ⟦Security⟧ «⟦Private⟧» with only your own user; NFS likewise.

Not you and no tool of yours: act now — take the server off the network, look at the logins in the night watchman's watch book, keep what is left (Ms. Snapshotini can hold it). Yours (zfs destroy by hand, a tool with its own retention): «All right, remember this» on his page — snapshots named like these may go from then on, as long as a newer one of the same kind stays.

check.snap_hold_released_how: A hold keeps a snapshot from being deleted — releasing it is the step before. You or a tool of yours (zfs release, a replication tool): «All right, this time» on the night watchman's page. If not: look at the logins in his watch book now and keep what is still held.

adopt.snap_hold_released: «All right, this time»: a hold released later is told again.

detail.evidence_none_snap: Nothing about zfs, btrfs, snapshots, plugins or scripts in the syslog then.

watch.snaps_asleep: asleep — compared once it is awake, no disk is woken

help.snaps_text: An attacker deletes the snapshots first, then encrypts. So at every check he compares the snapshots of the awake pools and disks, sleeping ones once they are awake. What the office removes itself he doesn't tell. Everything else goes into the watch book and to Unraid's notifications; the entry names who ran zfs destroy, and when. A released hold is told too, unless Ms. Snapshotini released it. «All right, remember this» teaches him a retention of yours: such snapshots may go as long as a newer one stays.

check.log_cleared_how: Wiping logs is what an intruder does to hide what happened. If it wasn't you or a plugin you know of: look at what happened just before — the other entries in the watch book, the logins, Ms. Protocolli.

check.user_ram_how: Unraid's accounts are made under ⟦Users⟧ and kept on the flash. An account only in RAM, a second user with UID 0 (root's rights), or a system account that may suddenly log in, is how intruders keep a way in. Look at /etc/passwd in Unraid's terminal; a reboot puts Unraid's own accounts back.

check.listen_new.other: {n} programs newly listen on network ports, the newest: {prog} on {port}

check.listen_new_how: A new door into the server. A plugin or a service you started yourself: «All right, remember this». A program you don't know: find it with ss -tlnp in Unraid's terminal.

check.proc_odd.other: {n} programs run from scratch folders, the newest: {prog} from {exe}

check.proc_odd_how: Programs normally live in /usr, or in their container's image. One started from /tmp, /dev/shm or from memory is how downloaded tools and miners run. If you don't know it: ps -ef in Unraid's terminal (or docker top for a container), and where it came from.

help.host_text: What a security team watches on a Linux server, as far as it says something on Unraid — at every check, from RAM. He tells logs emptied or replaced, new accounts and accounts with root rights, programs listening on a new port, and programs running from /tmp or a hidden folder. What is there at his first check counts as known. He also tells new ways in from outside: SSH, UPnP, Unraid Connect's remote access, WireGuard tunnels. Likewise new API keys or more rights for one; he never sees a key's value. What closes or is revoked he settles by himself.
help.host_not: What a SOC would also do — and why not here
help.host_not_text: Checking system files, scanning for viruses, inspecting network traffic, reading DNS and SMB login logs: on Unraid that is only noise, wakes every disk, floods /var/log or needs tools of its own. He switches nothing on for it.
help.attack_text: Each entry carries its nearest technique from MITRE ATT&CK — the catalogue security teams use to name what attackers do (T1053.003: a scheduled job in cron, T1070.002: logs cleared …). MITRE's catalogue lists it under this code. Nearest, not exact: a new plugin is software that runs as root at every boot.

Set up by you: «All right, remember this». If not: switch it off where it was switched on (⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Management Access⟧, ⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦VPN Manager⟧) and look at the logins.

chain.how: A login from a new address and soon after a way to stay (a cron line, a plugin, a port, an account), or snapshots gone and much written into a share — that is how intrusions and ransomware look. If it was you: answer the entries, and the box goes.

help.chain_text: Several important entries within an hour may belong to one incident, such as a new login and soon after a new cron line. He shows them together in each area that holds one of them, and Unraid's notifications get a message. Once an entry is done, it leaves the chain.

help.parity_text: Every parity check gets an entry with its reason: an unclean stop, schedule, by hand, or unknown. After an unclean stop he names what held up the array when «⟦Shutdown time-out⟧» ran out, and the team lead says which time-out to raise. He never starts or stops a check.
detail.logins_none: The syslog names no WebGUI or SSH login from half an hour before to five minutes after. It never says who clicked.
detail.logins_how: From the syslog: who logged in to the WebGUI or by SSH from half an hour before to five minutes after — the syslog never says who clicked.

round.night_flash: After a reboot: from his baseline on the flash.
help.night_text: While the array is stopped, the messenger rests, because his data lies on the pool. Then the night shift keeps watch, every five minutes, from RAM and the flash only: logins, the flash, plugins and what starts on its own. Containers, shares and snapshots wait for the array. It reports to Unraid's notifications as usual. When the array starts, its entries come into the watch book with the label «night shift». There is a night shift only after his first check.

If not: end the partnership at the Team Lead, pair anew (that writes the line as it should be) and look at the logins.

help.net_text: If your router sends its log to Unraid's syslog server, he reads it at every check. The Consultant shows how. That works with UniFi gateways and MikroTik routers (RouterOS 7). Only what concerns this server is told: new devices on the LAN, someone using the server's name or address, new router or VPN logins, changes to the firewall or port forwarding, attacks on the server, and the router's log going silent. From a MikroTik also internet outages and restarts. He wakes no disk and never says a word to the router.
help.net_not_text: Your router's log names every device. He keeps only what concerns this server. Other devices he names only when they are new or take the server's place. With «Whole LAN» he counts connections and detections per device, never a destination.

serious_text: He records the entry as an incident; in the watch book you find it under «Only incidents». Nothing of it counts as all right: if it is still there, he tells it again. While it stands there as an incident, the same from the same source is reported at once and as important — even what he otherwise only writes down — and never settled by himself or through the team lead. Was it you, or something you expected? Then «All right, remember this» is the answer. You can take it back later in the watch book with «Not an incident after all …».

serious_undo_title: Then it is no longer an incident: the same from the same source is told as usual again, and it ends as with «All right, remember this».

hold.how.userscript: Let it finish, or abort it in User Scripts.
hold.how.plugin: Let it finish — the plugin's own page says what it is doing.
hold.how.cron: Let it finish — it started on its own schedule.
hold.how.loop: Unmount the image before you stop the array.
hold.how.program: Let it finish, or end it before you stop the array.
hold.waits_sub: Unraid stops them itself before it unmounts: its own containers all at once within «⟦Docker Stop Timeout⟧» ({docker} s), the others with Docker itself, each VM within «⟦VM shutdown time-out⟧» ({vm} s) — then it turns the VM off hard.
hold.vm_agent_connected_title: Unraid's request to shut down goes to the guest agent: the VM shuts down cleanly and quickly
hold.vm_agent_disconnected_title: The VM has the guest agent's channel, but nothing answers in it: the agent isn't installed or isn't running
hold.vm_agent_none_title: The VM has no channel for the guest agent: only the power-button request reaches it
hold.vm_paused_title: Unraid resumes a paused VM first, then asks it to shut down
hold.vm_wait_title: Unraid waits up to {s} s for it («⟦VM shutdown time-out⟧»), then turns it off hard
hold.vm_windows: Without a guest agent that answers, Windows often ignores the first request to shut down — Unraid then waits all {s} s and turns it off hard. Install the VirtIO guest tools in Windows.
hold.vm_no_agent: Without a guest agent that answers only the power-button request reaches it; if the system in it ignores that, Unraid waits all {s} s and turns it off hard.
hold.ct_unraid_title: Unraid stops its containers with «⟦Docker Stop Timeout⟧» ({s} s), whatever their own stop time
hold.ct_compose_title: Not one of Unraid's containers (Compose, another tool): it stops with Docker itself, with its own stop time, up to {s} s
hold.ct_short_title: Its own stop time is {own} s, it gets {s} s — then it is killed: a database in it may not finish writing
hold.itself_sub: Unraid or the office ends these when the array stops.
hold.itself_office_title: The office's work ends by itself when the array stops — it never holds the array
hold.itself_mover_title: Unraid stops the mover first when the array stops
hold.itself_smb_title: Unraid closes Samba before it unmounts
hold.itself_nfs_title: Unraid closes NFS before it unmounts
hold.itself_syslog_title: Unraid closes its syslog server's files in the share before it unmounts
hold.files_open_title: Open on the array right now
hold.smb_text: Save what is open there first — Unraid closes Samba when the array stops.
hold.outside_sub: Other machines' shares and Unassigned Devices never hold the array; one that doesn't answer only makes the stop slower.
hold.out_remote_title: A share of another machine (/mnt/remotes): it never holds the array
hold.out_ud_title: A disk outside the array (/mnt/disks): it never holds the array
hold.snaps_sub: A look into a share's .zfs/snapshot folder mounts that snapshot; ZFS unmounts it again after about five minutes. When the array stops, Unraid unmounts the pools' datasets — a snapshot still mounted in one can make that wait («dataset is busy»).
hold.snaps_host_title: Mounted in a share's .zfs/snapshot folder on the server
hold.snaps_container_title: Mounted inside the container only — the server doesn't see it, and ZFS can't unmount it from out here
hold.snaps_process_title: Mounted only in a process's own view of the mounts — the server doesn't see it, and ZFS can't unmount it from out here
help.hold_text: What would hold up the array if you stopped it now? If a program has a file open on a disk, a pool or a share, Unraid can't unmount it. When «⟦Shutdown time-out⟧» runs out, the server shuts down unclean and the next start checks parity. VMs and containers Unraid stops itself. He only reads and wakes no disk.
wakes.title: Who woke my disks?
wakes.sub: Who wakes spinning disks? While a disk sleeps, every {s} s he looks who needs it. He only watches and never wakes a disk.
wakes.not_yet: I start watching as soon as the messenger runs this version.
wakes.no_hdd: No disk spins here — nothing that could sleep and be woken.
wakes.disk_only_title: Unfold the wakes of {disk} right here
wakes.none: No disk woke in the last 7 days.
wakes.note: Watching since {when} — every {s} s while a disk sleeps. Kept for 7 days.
wakes.cause.none_title: Nobody was waiting for the disk when he looked — whatever it was came and went within the spin-up.
wakes.sure.sure_title: It was waiting for the disk while it spun up, with a file on that disk open.
wakes.sure.likely_title: It was waiting while the disk spun up, with a file in a user share open — a share that can lie on this disk.
wakes.sure.maybe_title: It was waiting for a disk while this one spun up, without a file under /mnt he could see.
wakes.sure.open_title: Nobody was caught waiting; this one had a file open on the disk, or in a share that lies on it.
wakes.more_title: Unfold the row: everybody he caught then
wakes.cut_title: The server was busy: I stopped looking early to stay light — somebody may be missing.
wakes.how.caught: The time is when he saw somebody waiting for the disk.
wakes.how.syslog: Nobody was waiting when he looked; the time is from Unraid's syslog («read SMART» right after the spin-up).
wakes.how.noticed: Nobody was waiting when he looked; Unraid's list of disks says it woke between {from} and {to}.
wakes.naming: The names follow in a moment.
help.wakes_text: Unraid only logs when a spinning disk goes to sleep, never who wakes it. So while it sleeps he looks every few seconds. Whoever needs it has to wait while it spins up, and that is when he catches them: a container, a VM, a computer over SMB or NFS, the mover, a scheduled task, the office's own work or a program, with its open files. «Not found out» means nobody was waiting any more when he looked. He never wakes a disk. He watches only spinning disks: SSDs and NVMe never count, and a server with only those has nothing here.
wakes.switch_title: On unless you switch it off: while a disk sleeps he looks every few seconds. Off, he looks at nothing — what he noticed stays.
wakes.switched_off: Switched off — he doesn't watch any more; what he noticed stays.
wakes.off_note: Switched off: he doesn't watch for wakes now. What he noticed before stays here.
wakes.by.session: started in a terminal or SSH session
wakes.sure.wrote_title: It had written to a file on this disk shortly before. The server writes such data out a little later — that can wake the disk without anybody waiting for it.
wakes.unraid: Right after it woke, Unraid looked at it (its SMART values, whether it spins) — that is Unraid's answer to the wake, not its cause.
wakes.how.asked: The time is when he saw the disk being asked for.
wakes.trail_verdict_title: Nobody was caught waiting for the disk. Just then these files were written on it — a hint who woke it, not proof.
wakes.trail_verdict_maybe_title: He caught only someone waiting while it spun up, with no file of theirs there. Just then these files were written on it — a clue who woke it, no proof.
wakes.trail_also_title: It waited for a disk while it spun up, but held no file there he could see — less telling than what was written.
wakes.trail_head: Written on it right then — a hint, not proof:
wakes.trail_cut: I stopped looking early to stay light — more may have been written.
wakes.trail_walk: This disk keeps no list of its changes: I looked for files in the folders that changed since it slept — a file changed in place in an older folder can be missing.
wakes.trail_nothing: I found no file written on it then.

cat.why.hold_never: Not looked yet since the server started.

cat.why.hw_silent: His last look at the hardware is too old: its counters weren't read lately.

cat.why.hw_nvme_warning: An NVMe reports a critical warning (SMART).
cat.why.hw_worn: An SSD has used up the part of its life you set.

cat.why.vuln_never: Switched on, the lists not fetched yet — the first fetch is still to come.
cat.why.vuln_old: The lists are older than three days: not checked right now.

help.lights_text: Each area is a tile with a light: red — something waits for your answer; yellow — something to look at, or he couldn't look; green with «!» — fine, with advice or a part not checked; green — fine; grey — nothing to watch here, or switched off. Each light has its own shape, too. The filter above the row shows only the areas whose words fit, or only those where something waits for you. The mouse over a tile shows its first details.
help.read_text: The Night Watchman checks the server every five minutes, also while this page is closed. He changes nothing and wakes no disk. He remembers what he knows and tells only what is new or different.
help.read_lights_text: Each tile is an area; its colour says whether something waits for you there. Red: something waits for your answer, and it is urgent. Yellow: something waits for your answer, it isn't urgent. Green: all quiet. Green with «!»: all quiet, he has an advice for you. Grey: not checked — switched off, not there, or he can't reach it right now.
help.read_answers_text: «All right, remember this»: he remembers exactly this and no longer tells it; if it changes, he tells you again. «Something like this is always all right …»: you choose what he no longer tells from now on, for example everything from your home network. «That was an incident …»: he records it; if the same comes again, he tells it at once. You can take back every answer: in the area's setup, an incident in the watch book.
help.read_where_text: What waits for you: in its area, at the top. What he knows: in the area under «Known». What is done: in the watch book. What he no longer tells, and from when he tells: in the setup.
help.read_notify_text: What is urgent he sends to Unraid's notifications. They arrive wherever you send them in Unraid: ⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Notification Settings⟧ (browser, e-mail, or under ⟦Notification Agents⟧ Gotify, ntfy, Pushover and others). How often and at what time, you set at the Team Lead.
help.read_areas_more: Also the watch book with everything done and the schedule: when he checks and whether it works. In each area, «What he checks here» says what he looks at and when he tells you.

scope.login.tell_2: {burst} failed attempts from one address within {window}.

scope.login.tell_7: What the Team Lead writes when pairing or on «Change address», he records in the watch book himself.

scope.access.tell_4: What closes or gets tighter, he remembers without an entry.
scope.access.tell_5: If you want, ⟦Secure⟧ counts as all right, then he tells only ⟦Public⟧. The flash he always tells.
scope.access.tell_6: A partner's key that the Team Lead adds when pairing, he records in the watch book himself.
scope.access.tell_7: Telnet, FTP, UPnP and API keys with all rights stand as advice in this area.

scope.container.look_1: Every container and its special rights: privileged, the server's network or processes, extra capabilities, devices, Docker itself or the whole file system.
scope.container.look_2: Also the ports a container opens.
scope.container.tell_1: A new container with special rights.
scope.container.tell_2: A known container that newly runs privileged or with the server's network or processes.
scope.container.tell_3: Without a notification: new ports and other new rights of a known container (adjustable).
scope.container.tell_4: What gets less, he remembers without an entry.
scope.container.tell_5: A new container without special rights is all right. If you want, he records it in the watch book too.
scope.container.tell_6: What the Consultant creates through Unraid's form and Mr. Restori's practice containers, he records in the watch book himself.

scope.plugins.look_1: The installed plugins and where each gets its updates from. He reads only the files on the server and fetches nothing from the internet.
scope.plugins.look_2: What starts by itself: cron lines, the plugins' schedules, User Scripts, jobs for later (at) and Unraid's notification agents.
scope.plugins.look_3: What runs at boot: the go file, the packages in /boot/extra, the plugin files on the flash, the boot line, the kernel and other boot files (stop, modprobe.d, smb-extra.conf).
scope.plugins.tell_1: A new plugin, or one that suddenly gets its updates from somewhere else. That is the sign of a slipped-in source.
scope.plugins.tell_2: A new cron line or a duplicate of Unraid's own, a schedule of a plugin that isn't installed at all, a new or changed notification agent.

scope.plugins.tell_3.one: An unknown at job. If it still hasn't run one day after its time, it counts as stuck.
scope.plugins.tell_3.other: An unknown at job. If it still hasn't run {n} days after its time, it counts as stuck.

scope.plugins.tell_4: Every change to the go file, the packages and the boot files. An update of Unraid or a plugin through the plugin manager is all right.
scope.plugins.tell_5: Without a notification: changed schedules of installed plugins, new or changed User Scripts (adjustable).
scope.plugins.tell_6: What is removed, he remembers without an entry. If you want, spaces and comments in the go file don't count.
scope.plugins.tell_7: A new version from the same source is all right. If you want, he records it in the watch book.
scope.plugins.tell_8: What the office installs or schedules itself, what User Scripts start in the background and a plugin's own jobs, he records in the watch book himself.

scope.server.look_1: Which programs listen on a TCP port that isn't only internal.
scope.server.look_2: Programs that run from /tmp, /dev/shm, a hidden folder or straight from memory, on the server or in containers.
scope.server.look_3: Whether syslog, wtmp, btmp or lastlog were emptied or replaced, and /etc/ld.so.preload.
scope.server.look_4: In the syslog: a program the kernel ends for lack of memory, a service that crashes, very many connection attempts.
scope.server.look_5: When the server boots, and who was logged in at that time.
scope.server.tell_2: A program from such a place, as soon as it runs at two checks in a row.
scope.server.tell_3: A log that was emptied, not by its usual rotation. Every change to ld.so.preload.
scope.server.tell_4: Without a notification: memory full, a service that crashes {crashes} times in one hour, very many connection attempts (all adjustable).
scope.server.tell_5: A boot of the server, he records in the watch book himself.
scope.server.when_1: Every 5 minutes, at night too. The programs only when Docker answers.
scope.data.look_1: How much the server sends to each machine, over SMB, NFS, SSH and the web UI, and how much each container sends.
scope.data.look_2: How much is written into the shares, how much vanishes from them and how many files are deleted. On ZFS per share, on XFS and btrfs per disk.
scope.data.look_3: For each machine, container and share he learns what is usual. For machines and containers per hour of the week.

scope.data.tell_2: Written or gone: more than {d_factor} times the usual in one hour, and at least {written_min} written or {gone_min} gone. Or at least {files_min} deleted files.

scope.data.tell_4: Always, even if you marked something like this as always all right: half a share gone, or 200 000 deleted files in one hour.
scope.data.tell_5: What a snapshot still holds counts as gone (adjustable).
scope.data.tell_6: Backups, the mover, Ms. Moverelli, Jack Streamer and the transfers to partners don't count. Emby, Jellyfin and Plex he only learns and never judges.

scope.snap.tell_2: A hold that Ms. Snapshotini did not release.
scope.snap.tell_3: The offsite copy has fewer than {offsite} % of the snapshots from last time.

scope.net.look_1: Your router's log, if it sends it to Unraid's syslog server. He understands UniFi, MikroTik and netfilter and keeps only what concerns this server.
scope.net.look_2: From it: logins to the router, firewall and forwards, VPN logins, new devices in the LAN, detections of the intrusion prevention (IPS) and connections the router blocks.
scope.net.look_3: Even without a router log: through which router the server goes to the internet (its MAC address), and which DNS servers it asks.
scope.net.tell_1: A router admin he doesn't know or who comes from a new address. Repeated failed attempts at the router.
scope.net.tell_2: Changes to firewall, NAT or port forwards. A VPN login from a new user or a new address.
scope.net.tell_3: Someone poses as this server, an IPS detection involving this server, or a blocked connection from the server to the outside.

scope.net.tell_6: Without a notification: new devices, other DNS servers, connection drops, internet outages and restarts (adjustable). He tells them when they pile up, last long or were unclean.
scope.net.tell_7: On the first read, the log so far counts as known. Other people's devices he knows only as numbers, unless you switch on «Whole LAN».

scope.net.when_2: The router and the DNS servers at night too.

scope.net.example_2: The router 192.168.1.1 answers with a different MAC address: …
scope.hw.look_1: Error counters: hardware errors of the CPU (machine checks), memory errors (ECC), PCIe errors, throttling from heat and the kernel's warning flags.
scope.hw.look_2: Temperatures over hours: NVMe, CPU and the disks that are awake right now. Also Unraid's own SMART values and read and write errors in the syslog.
scope.hw.look_3: CPUs with a known flaw and old microcode. All from memory, without tools, and no disk wakes up for it.
scope.hw.tell_1: Every machine check. A memory or PCIe error that was not corrected, or {ecc_day} corrected memory errors in one day.
scope.hw.tell_3: Too warm for hours: NVMe {nvme_time} above {nvme_c} °C, disks {disk_time} above {disk_c} °C, the CPU {cpu_time} above its limit.
scope.hw.tell_4: SMART warning signs that grow (5, 187, 188, 197, 198), critical NVMe warnings, read and write errors of a disk.
scope.hw.tell_5: Without a notification: fewer corrected errors, throttling, and an SSD that is {worn} % worn.
scope.hw.tell_6: What the server doesn't have, he calls «not available», never «0 errors».

check.hw_mce_how: A machine check is the processor itself reporting an error in the CPU, its caches, the memory controller or a bus — no program can cause one. A single one can be chance; more, or together with crashes, point at the CPU, the memory, the power supply or a BIOS setting (overclocking, undervolting). Look in the syslog for «Hardware Error» around that time, run a memory test, update the BIOS and check the CPU's temperatures.

check.hw_ecc_how: ECC memory corrects single wrong bits and counts them. A few corrected ones a month are normal; many a day, or more and more on one module, mean that module is starting to fail — plan to replace it. Hundreds an hour, or any that could not be corrected, point at the card or drive, its slot, a riser cable or the link's power saving (ASPM). check.hw_kernel_how: The kernel marks itself when something went wrong inside it; the marks stay until the next start: D a crash (an Oops or a BUG), B a bad memory page, M a machine check, L a CPU that hung, W a warning. A warning alone is often a driver's complaint; the others point at the hardware or a faulty driver. Look in the syslog for «Oops», «BUG», «soft lockup» or «WARNING» around that time; after a crash a restart is the safe way back.

posture.cpu_fault.title: {cpu}: a known fault ({fault}) — its microcode {microcode} is older than the correction ({min})
posture.cpu_fault.why: Intel's 13th and 14th Gen desktop CPUs can age under too high a voltage until they crash and hang. Intel's correction is microcode {min} or newer, and it comes with a BIOS update — Intel says it must be loaded that way, together with the BIOS's «Intel Default Settings». Update the board's BIOS to one that has it. A microcode doesn't heal a CPU already harmed: repeated crashes and hangs are the sign, and then the CPU goes back under its warranty, which Intel extended to up to five years. Machine checks since the server's start: {mce} — the area Hardware shows them and the kernel's crashes.
posture.old_microcode.title: {cpu} started with old microcode ({microcode})
posture.old_microcode.why: The kernel keeps a list of the microcode the makers released; this CPU started with older microcode than that (the kernel's own word: old_microcode «Vulnerable»). Newer microcode closes security holes or fixes faults of the CPU. It comes with a BIOS update of the board, or with an Unraid version that brings newer microcode — look for a BIOS update first.

check.hw_wear_how: From Unraid's own SMART reading — no disk was woken for it. Reallocated, pending or uncorrectable sectors (5, 197, 198), reported uncorrectable errors (187) and command timeouts (188) that grow are the forerunners of a failing disk: make sure its data is in a backup and plan to replace it. An NVMe's critical warning or media errors mean the same for an SSD. CRC errors (199) are mostly the cable or the backplane; unsafe shutdowns are lost power (a parity check follows). More than 100 % of life used is no defect by itself — the drive estimates it.

help.setup_rules_text: What is always all right he writes down but never tells. For the data flow it can also set when he tells (only from an amount, a snapshot's hold, new Docker images). On an entry he suggests narrow cases; here you add wider ones by hand — a net, a share, a series of snapshots, a router's admin. Always told: more than half of a share gone or 200 000 files deleted in one hour (unless you switch that off). «Tell again» is honest: at his next check he tells what is still different.
help.history_text: What he settles himself, or doesn't tell because it is always all right, leaves the watch book after a quiet week. Then it stays 13 months in his history, by month — under the book, loaded when you open it. The book keeps what is open and what you answered.

ack_title: He remembers exactly this and no longer tells it. If it changes, he tells you again.
serious_title: He records it; nothing of it counts as all right. If the same comes again, he tells it at once.
rule.always: Something like this is always all right …
undo.ack: Remembered. He no longer tells it, unless it changes.
undo.ack_once: Ticked off. If it happens again, he tells it again.

undo.ack_all.one: Done. He no longer tells it, unless it changes.
